newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africa rand/bonds closing report.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa rand/bonds closing report.

text.p: The South African rand was whipped higher in hectic late trade as local exporters and offshore banks moved in decisively to sell dollars, sparking a rush for cover by speculators long of the U.S. unit.
"For the first time in quite a while we've seen export dollars coming into the market -- and there have been some really pretty substantial orders," one dealer said.
Traders said the market had been very long of dollars and the rand's failure to breach decisively the 4.70 level had caused some players to cut positions given high carrying costs.
London banks, in particular, came in as big dollar sellers in the afternoon. Some dealers also saw the indirect hand of the Reserve Bank in the rand's sharp retracement, though others were sceptical.
The rand's recovery fuelled a similar advance in the bond market with yields pulling back smartly after earlier hitting five-month highs.

Dealers said high short-term rates and fears of an official rate hike continued to over-shadow the market. But some said there could now be a flow of funds from equities to bonds given that high rates would choke off company earnings growth.
"The foreigners are still largely staying away but we could see some domestic funds switching out of equities into bonds," said one dealer.
The rand ended at 4.6785/35 against the dollar from 4.7020/70 on Monday. Against the crosses, the rand was at 7.7092/7222 against sterling from 7.7350/7494 and at 0.3201/06 marks against 0.3195/99.
The government's R150 long bond issue ended at the day's best level of 16.09 percent bid after yields moved as high as 16.24 earlier.
That represented a nine basis point advance on Monday's 16.18 close -- but dealers noted bonds had still done little to recover from Monday's huge 35 basis point kick-up in yields.

The daily money market shortage eased back marginally on Monday to 9.110 billion rand from 9.191 billion on Saturday. But dealers saw no relief for three-month money while the shortage remained above nine billion.
The high shortage, reflecting a liquidity squeeze in the wake of the latest sell-off in the rand and South African assets, has fuelled fears of a hike in interest rates.
Short-term rates, which were marked up sharply on Monday, are already more than discounting a one percentage point increase in the key Bank rate, currently 16 percent.
On Tuesday, commercial banks held their three-month NCD rates steady at between 16.85 and 17.10 percent, while the 90-day BA rate was unchanged at 16.25 to 16.45 percent.
Money market traders said pressure on liquidity would continue until around the end of January as Christmas spending was likely to exacerbate the situation.

The Bond Exchange said foreigners bought a net 79.04 million rand worth of South African bonds on Monday after selling a net 4.66 million rand on Friday. Nominal cumulative volumes stood at 5.93 billion rand on Monday from 2.92 billion rand on Friday.
